summary: A console-driven workshop focused on how Redwood Optimize suggests and applies quantization profiles (INT8 vs FP8), how fallback rules and rollout policies work for edge-case prompts, and a plan to run a 2-week sandbox pilot. Customer concerned about rare failure modes and latency SLOs across mixed load.
topics: Console Optimize recommendations and heatmap visualization
Fallback policies and canary rollouts for qprofile changes
Latency vs quality tradeoffs and real-world example prompts
Sandbox pilot plan and security/VPC considerations
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Alright everyone good afternoon, thanks for hopping on. I'm Maya, AE for Redwood Inference, with Liam from our SE team. Today's goal is a hands-on console walkthrough — how Optimize suggests quantization profiles and how you can protect production with fallback rules.
[00:14] Aisha Patel: Hi, Maya. Appreciate it. We're especially worried about those edge-case prompts that spike hallucinations when we drop precision. So we wanna see the console, and then the fallback behavior.
[00:25] Liam O'Neill: Totally. We'll demo INT8 vs FP8 profiles and an example where the system auto-falls back to a higher-precision variant if quality regression is detected. Quick context check — are you running a 3k token max, or shorter sequences?
[00:36] Marco Reyes: Most of our calls are 512 tokens or less, but we do have a long-form summarization pipeline that hits ~2k occasionally.
[00:44] Noah Stein: From infra, we'll need to confirm VPC peering for the sandbox. Also curious about audit logs retention and KMS integration.
[00:52] Maya Chen: Great, we'll show the security panel too. Quick agenda: 1) Console Optimize heatmap + profile suggestions, 2) Live qprofile import/apply, 3) Failure mode + fallback demo, 4) Rollout policy and canary, 5) Q&A.
[01:05] Liam O'Neill: Jumping in — here's the Optimize tab. The heatmap aggregates token-level sensitivity and shows suggested precision per layer. You'll see a suggested INT8 profile for most traffic, but it flags layers with high activation variance as 'sensitive' and proposes FP8 there.
[01:24] Marco Reyes: Wait, that layer naming looks different — it says L-23 attn -> is that matching our model, or is that Redwood's internal mapping?
[01:32] Liam O'Neill: It's a mapping. For open models we surface the layer index, occasionally the names get noisy in transcription — the console maps to your model after import.
[01:40] Aisha Patel: How does Optimize determine sensitivity? Is this a calibration dataset you provide, or does Redwood sample live traffic?
[01:48] Liam O'Neill: Both. We start with a small calibration sweep over your sample prompts (we ask for 500–2k examples), then recommend a qprofile. After deployment, we continuously monitor quality and token-level perplexity; if drift's detected, Optimize suggests adjustments or an automatic fallback.
[02:03] Noah Stein: Automatic fallback — does that route to a different model or just adjust precision on the fly? Concerned about capacity during fallback.
[02:12] Liam O'Neill: Two options: 1) precision fallback (switch to FP8 or FP16 on the same instance) if hardware supports it, or 2) route to a higher-tier model variant in a different pool — e.g., from INT8-optimized variant to FP8-optimized variant, or to a dedicated low-latency pool if you have Dedicated capacity. We show both policies in the console.
[02:32] Maya Chen: For capacity, we can set cost thresholds so fallback only occurs if p99 latency remains under a set SLO, otherwise it can fall back to a lower-cost tolerance rule — it's configurable.
[02:43] Marco Reyes: Could you show a real example? Maybe one of our security-scan prompts which triggered hallucinations in prior runs.
[02:50] Liam O'Neill: Yep — pulling up the prompt set you shared earlier. Here's prompt 'sec-scan-07' — baseline (FP16) accuracy score 0.92. When we apply INT8 profile suggested by Optimize, quality drops to 0.84 on that prompt. Console flags it as a regression on the quality dashboard.
[03:08] Aisha Patel: That's the crux. We can tolerate a small drop for 95% of traffic, but those 5% wrong answers are unacceptable.
[03:16] Liam O'Neill: Understood. In the rollout policy we'll create a rule: if quality delta > 0.05 for any prompt in the 'safety-critical' tag, automatically pin those prompts to FP8/FP16 and exclude from the INT8 route. So you get mixed-precision routing at request granularity.
[03:34] Noah Stein: Mixed routing — how's that implemented? I assume it's request metadata-based? We don't want to inspect user content on Redwood side for privacy reasons.
[03:42] Maya Chen: Good point. The route decision can be made either client-side (your service tags the request with a profile hint) or server-side with an opaque hash of prompt ID — we never store raw PII, and you can opt into local-only decisioning. We'll document options in the security whitepaper.
[03:58] Marco Reyes: Can we do a canary roll? Like 5% traffic on INT8, watch quality for 72 hours, then ramp?
[04:06] Liam O'Neill: Absolutely — the console has a rollout slider. You can define stages, duration, automatic rollback thresholds (quality delta, error rate, latency). We'll demo a 10% canary now.
[04:18] [05:00] Demo: Liam initiates a 10% INT8 canary. The console graph shows token latency and quality delta streaming in.
[05:15] Marco Reyes: Seeing a small bump in p95 latency but nothing catastrophic. The problem prompt still shows regression.
[05:25] Maya Chen: Now watch the fallback in action — because that prompt is tagged 'safety-critical', the routing rules immediately switch that request to FP8 variant; note the console indicates a per-request exception.
[05:40] Aisha Patel: Nice. So the majority of traffic benefits from INT8 cost reductions, but we never sacrifice safety-critical outputs.
[05:47] Liam O'Neill: Correct. On the pricing side, typical INT8 can be 30–50% cheaper per token; FP8 sits in between INT8 and FP16. We'll include an estimated cost delta in the sandbox report.
[05:59] Marco Reyes: How reproducible are quality metrics? We ran a local quant sweep and saw non-deterministic variations — sometimes INT8 looked fine, sometimes not.
[06:08] Liam O'Neill: Quantization sensitivity can vary with input distribution and temperature settings. Optimize runs multiple seed-based evaluation sweeps and reports confidence intervals. It also surfaces prompt clusters that are high variance.
[06:20] Noah Stein: Regarding hardware, do you support dynamic kernel swaps or do we need separate instances for FP8?
[06:27] Liam O'Neill: On most modern GPUs we can toggle kernels at runtime if the driver supports it, but in many cases we prefer to keep separate instance flavors that are tuned per-precision to avoid cold path penalties. We show both options and their latency profiles.
[06:41] Aisha Patel: Can Redwood's runtime do partial layer mixed precision? Like INT8 for most layers but FP8 for the top few?
[06:49] Liam O'Neill: Yes — Optimize can generate fine-grained qprofiles with per-layer precision. We present a compact profile that says [layers 0-10: INT8, 11-18: FP8, 19-24: FP16] — the runtime applies it efficiently and the console visualizes expected latency impact.
[07:05] Marco Reyes: Any gotchas on tokenizer behavior or KV cache when mixing precision?
[07:11] Liam O'Neill: Tokenization is orthogonal. KV cache is precision-aware; when swapping precision mid-session we might need to rekey the cache or warm it — Optimize flags long-running sessions that would be negatively impacted.
[07:22] Maya Chen: Quick pause for questions.
[07:27] Aisha Patel: On the security checklist — is the audit log itemized per-request and do you store request bodies?
[07:33] Maya Chen: By default we store metadata and hashes for auditability; you can enable full request logging in Private deployments or with an enterprise contract. For Hosted, we have redaction options and KMS integration. We'll send the SOC2 snippets in the whitepaper.
[07:46] Noah Stein: Sandbox networking — what's the expected egress pattern and IP addresses?
[07:51] Liam O'Neill: We'll provide a CIDR block and egress IP list, and VPC peering options. For on-prem/private deployments we can support air-gapped bundles but that requires a different engagement.
[08:03] Marco Reyes: Back to quality — can we manually override Optimize's suggestions? Sometimes we know domain-specific constraints.
[08:10] Liam O'Neill: Yes, the console supports manual qprofile upload and per-endpoint overrides. You can lock a profile per model/version, or set rules by route.
[08:19] Maya Chen: Okay, we're 35 minutes in — we'll run a short stress test next: synthetic burst of 100 concurrent requests to see batching behavior under INT8 vs FP8.
[08:29] [08:50] Demo: Synthetic workload applied. Console displays throughput, average tokens/sec, batching histogram.
[09:05] Marco Reyes: Interesting — INT8 shows slightly higher throughput but a tail latency bump. FP8 looks more stable in p99.
[09:15] Liam O'Neill: Exactly the classic tradeoff: INT8 wins cost and average throughput; FP8 improves tail and rare-case fidelity. That's why hybrid profiles plus routing rules are popular.
[09:27] Aisha Patel: What's the recommended rollout timeline? We have production traffic now; want to avoid regressions.
[09:33] Liam O'Neill: Common pattern: 1) calibration sweep on a curated sample (1–2 days), 2) 10% canary for 72 hours, 3) extend to 50% with automated checks for 1 week, 4) full rollout. The Optimize console templates this pipeline.
[09:47] Maya Chen: Let's capture specific metrics for your team: p95 latency target, acceptable quality delta for 'safety-critical' routes, and cost-savings target.
[09:56] Marco Reyes: p95 < 180ms, safety delta < 0.02, cost savings target 30%.
[10:03] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll tailor the qprofile and the rollout thresholds.
[10:08] Aisha Patel: Any limitations with custom ops or proprietary models? We run a few in-house variants.
[10:14] Liam O'Neill: For proprietary models we support importing weights and running the same Optimize flows in Private or Dedicated. Some custom kernels might need a short integration cycle. We'll flag those during onboarding.
[10:26] Noah Stein: Last question — alerting integration. Can we pipe quality regressions to PagerDuty?
[10:31] Maya Chen: Yes, we have webhook and PagerDuty integrations with templated alerts for quality, latency, and error spikes.
[10:38] Aisha Patel: Great. Sounds promising. Next step for us is to get the sandbox and the example qprofile.
[10:45] Maya Chen: Action items covered — we'll share the security doc and the qprofile. Liam will include a short screencast showing manual overrides and the canary flow.
[10:55] Liam O'Neill: One more note — there's a small chance of transcription mismatch in the console UI; some layer names can look odd (we call out the mapping). Don't hesitate to ask if something looks off.
[11:05] Marco Reyes: Thanks — looking forward to the sandbox.
[11:10] Aisha Patel: Thanks everyone.
[11:12] Maya Chen: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the pilot kickoff.
notes: Customer wants fine-grained fallback rules and mixed-precision routing. Security and VPC peering are blockers for sandbox; Redwood agreed to provide SOC2 excerpts and VPC CIDR. Qprofile showed a specific regression on 'sec-scan-07' that will be excluded from INT8 route.
